title: Why space flattens astronauts' eyeballs 👁️
subject: eye
description:
Would you trade your eyesight for 6 months in space? 👇

On long missions, fluid shifts toward the head and can flatten the back of the eyeball, swell the optic nerve and blur vision. NASA calls it spaceflight-associated neuro-ocular syndrome (SANS). In 2005, astronaut John Phillips came home with 20/100 vision. Not medical advice.

Sources: National Geographic, "Mystery of Astronauts' Blurry Vision May Finally Be Solved" (2016); Space.com, "Astronauts on the ISS experience vision changes" (2025); Université de Montréal study led by Santiago Costantino (2025); The Sunday Post (2016)
tags: what happens to your eyes in space

scenes.text: Space can flatten the back of your eyeballs.
In 2005, NASA astronaut John Phillips spent 6 months on the International Space Station.
Back home, his vision tested at 20/100. Before launch, it was 20/20.
Without gravity, fluid rises toward the head and presses on the eyes from behind.
A 2025 study of 13 astronauts found their eyeballs had become 33 percent less rigid.
Most cases improve on Earth. Phillips's eyes only got back to 20/50.
